standfirst: Nobody rewatches this for the paragliding accident. They rewatch it for Company Five: four soldiers learning what a face cream is, a village of women who gossip like a Greek chorus, and a man who plays piano badly for the woman he cannot keep. These six chase that mix of broad comedy and genuine grief, not the border plot.

picks.why: Same writer, same recipe. Park Ji-eun again: slapstick for eight hours, an ensemble of relatives who steal every scene, then a hard swerve into a weepie you did not consent to. The chaebol house replaces the North Korean village as the place where outsiders get slowly absorbed. Difference: the central couple starts already broken instead of falling in love, so the first four hours are colder.

Park Ji-eun's earlier version of the same engine: an impossible gap between two people, played for comedy before it is played for tears. Cheon Song-yi is the blueprint for every proud, ridiculous, secretly lonely heroine that followed. Difference: it is a 2013 SBS show and the production shows its age in ways CLOY never does.

The same fated-couple ache with time instead of a border in the way, and the same devoted male lead who quietly rearranges his whole life around one person. Warmer, funnier per minute, and it understands what being a fan of someone actually feels like in a way CLOY does not. Difference: much lighter emotional load and no political stakes at all.

If what you rewatch CLOY for is the banter and the second couple, this is that isolated and concentrated into twelve fast hours. Same webtoon-bright comedy, same competent-woman-meets-stiff-rich-man shape. Difference: it never once tries to make you cry, which is either the appeal or the dealbreaker.

The other side of the same wound: a divided Korea, an impossible love across a line drawn by history, and a scale that CLOY only gestures at. Kim Eun-sook writing at her most painterly. Difference: it is genuinely tragic and there is no comic relief village to come home to.

A fated trio, a supernatural conceit that exists mostly to force people into each other's lives, and a found family that ends up mattering more than the premise. Difference: half-hour episodes and a procedural rhythm, so it never builds one long unbroken sweep.

against.title: Descendants of the Sun
against.why: The default recommendation, and understandable: same writer-adjacent gloss, uniformed male lead, romance in a dangerous place. But the danger is decorative and there is no domestic ensemble. CLOY works because of the neighbours, and this has none.

against.title: The King: Eternal Monarch
against.why: Sold as the same thing with a bigger budget: two worlds, one impossible crossing. In practice the parallel-universe mechanics eat the romance alive, and the leads spend most of the runtime explaining the rules to each other.

against.title: Reply 1988
against.why: The other beloved one, so it gets paired here by default. It is beloved, and it also has no plot engine, no urgency and no forbidden anything. Come out of CLOY wanting momentum and you will stall by episode four.
